name: Zane Farah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm studying to be a secondary school maths and physics teacher. Weekdays are lectures and tutorials, and on Thursdays I help out in a Year 9 class at a school across town. I live at home with my parents and two younger sisters, and on Saturdays and Sunday afternoons I work at a hardware store, mostly the paint counter and stock. After that I run a small thing on the side, where I make phone stands and plant holders on a 3D printer my uncle lent me, and sell them online. We go to the mosque on Fridays and my mum cooks for half the street after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, let's use it for what it's actually good at. I'd tell my friends that I use AI every day, for planning lessons and getting past tricky physics problems, and that it doesn't change the main job. I'd say a teacher still has to know the subject and care about the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be relaxed about the world but not about money. My parents can't pay for much, and the loan covers fees only. I've got about a hundred pounds saved. What really matters to me is making the printing side business earn properly, so I'm not just relying on the hardware store.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on and push the side business harder. I'd make a proper online shop with better photos, and aim for about two hundred pounds a month. I'd keep the hardware shifts. I'd use the AI to write product descriptions and plan my lessons faster. I'd also ask the school where I help about holiday cover work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good, hungry. I like a stable world because I can plan a business in it, but I still feel the pinch every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does the side business work now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I make about forty items a month and sell around thirty at six to ten pounds. After material and the website fee, I clear maybe sixty pounds. It's small, but it's mine. My dad says a man should earn with his hands, and he's proud, even if he says it's a hobby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the thing you'd most want to improve?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The photos, honestly. People buy on pictures. I'd borrow my cousin's camera and learn to light the products. It's a cheap change, and I'm sure it would double my sales. Then I'd think about selling to local shops too.

say: Use it for what it's actually **good** at, because a teacher still has to know the subject and care about the kids.
I use AI every day for lesson plans and tricky physics problems.
think: I'm relaxed about the world but not about **money**, with about a hundred pounds saved.
The side business needs to earn properly so I'm not relying on the hardware store.
do: Build a proper online **shop** with better photos and aim for two hundred pounds a month.
Keep the hardware shifts and use AI for product descriptions and lesson plans.
Ask the school about holiday cover work.
feel: Good and **hungry**, because a stable world lets me plan, but I still feel the monthly pinch.
S0.quote: I make about forty items a month and sell around thirty at six to ten pounds.
fieldNote: Zane uses AI daily and answers a plateau by growing his **side** business, which clears about sixty pounds a month.
His father calls it a hobby but is proud, in line with his view that a man should earn with his hands.

steps.text: Build a proper online shop with better product photos
Use AI to write product descriptions and plan lessons
Keep the weekend hardware store shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for people who work hard and learn. I'd tell the lads at the store that they should learn the tools, and that no handout will replace being useful. I'd say it's fine to move around jobs, but that the family comes first, whatever happens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd feel pretty good about it, but I'd keep it to myself. Teaching has a lot of marking, planning and admin that AI can speed up, so schools might need fewer assistants, but they'd still need teachers. And my business could use the tools to grow faster, if I learn how.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go deeper on the tools, like using AI to mark practice quizzes and make revision packs. I'd start selling those revision packs to local students at four or five pounds each, which would be a second product. I'd keep the shifts at the store. And I'd look into a small business grant for the printing, since the council has one for young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited with a bit of nerves. It's like the starting gun for something. I'm not scared, but I know I need to move early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why revision packs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I've already got the maths and physics and I can check it myself. Parents pay for revision, it's an easy sale. At five pounds a pack, forty packs a month is two hundred pounds. I'd ask my Year 9 teacher what her students find hard, and make packs on that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about the changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That the people I'm close to won't catch up. My dad's shop is a repair garage, and his customers' orders will change. I'd teach him to use the booking tools. He'd moan, but he'd do it.

say: It's an **opportunity** for people who work hard and learn.
No handout will replace being useful, and family comes first, whatever happens.
think: I'd feel good about it privately: schools may need fewer assistants but still need **teachers**.
My business could grow faster if I learn the tools.
do: Use AI to mark practice quizzes and make **revision** packs.
Sell the packs to local students at four or five pounds each.
Look into the council's small business grant for young people.
feel: **Excited** with a bit of nerves, like a starting gun.
S1.quote: At five pounds a pack, forty packs a month is two hundred pounds.
fieldNote: Zane sees disruption as a **starting gun** and responds with a second product, revision packs, which he can check himself.
He worries about people close to him, like his father, who won't catch up.

steps.text: Sell maths and physics revision packs at five pounds each
Use AI to mark practice quizzes for the packs
Apply for the council's young business grant

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is serious, and that we've got to be ready to work harder and smarter. I'd tell friends to start something of their own, because waiting for a job to be handed to you won't work. At the mosque I'd say people should look after the elderly and the young.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared. Two years means I'd still be a trainee when the thinking work goes to AI. I'd worry that schools wouldn't need me, or that there'd be fewer of them. Mum and Dad rely on me to be the one who does well. I'd feel the weight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put everything into the business, and keep my degree going as a safety net. I'd take on more printing and sell revision packs, and I'd get a stall at the Saturday market. I'd save everything I could. I'd ask my uncle if I can use his workshop for bigger prints. And I'd pitch to schools, since robots are three years behind and kids still need someone to teach them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and driven. I'd sleep badly, but I'd get up early and work. That's how I get through fear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about your degree if the school jobs shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish it, because it's a good qualification, and then use it in a different way, like running a tutoring company or an online academy. Teaching skills still matter when AI does the content, because kids need someone to keep them going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does having only two years change the way you'd run the business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take more risks. I'd put a few hundred pounds into a better printer and take orders for local shops and offices. In a normal world I'd wait. With two years, if it works it works, and if not, I'd know quickly.

say: This is **serious**, and we have to work harder and smarter.
Start something of your own, because waiting for a job to be handed to you won't work.
think: I'd be scared: I'd still be a **trainee** when the thinking work goes to AI.
Mum and Dad rely on me to be the one who does well.
do: Put everything into the **business** and keep the degree as a safety net.
Get a stall at the Saturday market and pitch revision packs to schools.
Ask my uncle to let me use his workshop.
feel: Anxious and **driven**, sleeping badly but up early.
S2.quote: With two years, if it works it works, and if not, I'd know quickly.
fieldNote: Zane turns fear into **work**: stall, packs, bigger prints, all while keeping his degree as a net.
He believes teaching skills outlast AI content because kids need someone to keep them going.

steps.text: Get a Saturday market stall for the printed goods and packs
Spend a few hundred pounds on a better printer
Finish the teaching degree as a safety net
Save everything left after the printer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough if you move early. I'd tell people to learn the tools now and build something on the side. I'd also tell my uni they should teach how AI works in the classroom, since our pupils will use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'd feel optimistic. I'd graduate in about 2029 and have a couple of years of teaching before the robots arrive. And by then I'd have a small business with a few hundred a month. It's not guaranteed, but I'd be diversified, which feels safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my degree and teach, while building up the business at weekends. I'd save about fifty pounds a month, and put another fifty into better equipment. I'd ask the school if I could run an after-school club on 3D printing, which would be good for kids and my CV. And I'd learn to run ads for the online shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and a bit tense. I'd have enough time to build, but not enough time to waste.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the club look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Twelve kids, an hour a week, printing things like a bridge to test in physics. The school gives me a room, and I'd get a stipend or free printing materials. I'd get a reference and a reason to be known in the area. It'd also be fun.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What worries you about five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I get too comfortable. If the business ticks over and the teaching pays the rent, I might stop trying new things. I'd put a note on the wall to check every year if I'm still moving forward.

say: Five years is enough if you move **early**.
Learn the tools now and build something on the side.
think: I'd feel **optimistic**: a couple of years of teaching and a small business before the robots arrive.
Being diversified feels safe, though nothing is guaranteed.
do: Finish the degree and teach while building the business at **weekends**.
Save fifty pounds a month and put another fifty into equipment.
feel: Hopeful and a bit **tense**, with time to build but not to waste.
S3.quote: If the business ticks over and the teaching pays the rent, I might stop trying new things.
fieldNote: More time lets Zane **diversify**: teaching, a business and a school club that builds his name locally.
He names his own risk, getting too comfortable, and plans an annual check.

steps.text: Finish the degree and start teaching at a local school
Save fifty pounds a month from the hardware wage
Put another fifty a month into better printing equipment
Run an after-school 3D printing club at my school

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a lot of time and that I'm quite excited. I'd tell friends to get good at something real and not wait for permission. I'd say it's also a chance for families to look after each other better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I'd be calm. I'd have time to finish my degree, teach for years, grow a business and maybe marry. I'd be about twenty-nine when robots arrive, and I'd have a house if I'm lucky. My worry would be the same as it is now: not enough money in the first few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and teach. I'd build the business so it can work without me, maybe with a part-time helper. I'd save for a house with my future wife. I'd keep up with new tools every year, and I'd help my sisters through school and university.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hungry. It feels like a good time to be young and willing to work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you help your sisters?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Layla's fifteen and wants to be a vet, so I'd cover her books and some of the time costs. My other sister, Hana, is eleven, so I'd help her with maths now. It's my job as the eldest. My dad's proud of that, and my mum says I'm too serious.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently if you knew about the ten years in advance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the business earlier and bigger. I'd also talk to people who've built things, rather than learn by trial and error. And I'd save more, because ten years of compound growth beats a short scramble.

say: Ten years is a lot of time, so get good at something **real** and don't wait for permission.
It's also a chance for families to look after each other better.
think: I'd be **calm**, with time to finish my degree, teach, grow a business and maybe marry.
My worry would be not enough money in the first few years.
do: Finish the degree, teach and build the business so it works without **me**.
Save for a house with my future wife.
Help my sisters through school and university.
feel: Calm and **hungry**, a good time to be young and willing to work.
S4.quote: Ten years of compound growth beats a short scramble.
fieldNote: Zane thinks of ten years as room to build **systems**: a business that runs without him and support for his sisters.
His worry is the same as now: money in the first few years.

steps.text: Finish the degree and teach for several years
Build the printing business so a helper can run it
Help my sisters with books and maths

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Two years. That's the one where there's no space to build, and I'd rely on the business before it was ready. What would help is cheap loans for young people starting out, some honest news from my uni, and mentors who've built a business from nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being adaptable doesn't make me less worried about my family. I can move quickly but my parents can't. If the news is bad, I'm the one they'd lean on, and I'd want to be ready.

headlineQuote: I can move quickly but my parents can't. If the news is bad, I'm the one they'd lean on, and I'd want to be ready.
portrait: Zane is a 19-year-old **teaching** student who lives with his parents and sisters and works at a hardware store.
He is traditional and adaptive: he uses AI daily, believes in hard work and runs a small 3D printing business.
He answers every scenario by building something: shop, revision packs, a school club.
His main worry is his family, who cannot move as fast as he can.
biggestWorry: The **two-year** picture worries him most because there'd be no space to build, and his family would lean on him.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **loans** for young people starting out, honest news from his university, and mentors who have built a business.
